“Such reflections soothed me, and during the afternoon I fell into a deep slumber; yet the fever coursing in my blood denied me tranquil dreams. The dreadful events of the previous day were continually enacted before me: the women fleeing, and the furious Felix dragging me away from his father's feet. I woke wearied, and, perceiving that darkness had already fallen, stole out of my retreat to look for food.

“When I had satisfied my hunger, I turned towards the familiar path leading to the cottage. Everything there lay quiet. I slipped into my shed and waited silently for the usual hour at which the household rose. That hour went by; the sun climbed far into the sky, yet none of the cottagers appeared. I shook violently, fearing that some terrible calamity had occurred. Within the cottage all was dark, and no movement reached my ears; words cannot express the torment of that uncertainty.

“After a time two countrymen came past, stopping near the cottage to converse with vehement gestures. I could make nothing of their speech, for they used the language of the country, different from my protectors' own. Soon afterwards Felix came up accompanied by another man. This astonished me, since I knew he had not left the cottage that morning, and I listened eagerly for his conversation to explain these strange circumstances.

“‘Have you considered,’ his companion asked, ‘that you must pay three months' rent and forfeit everything your garden produces? I have no desire to profit unfairly, and therefore beg you to allow yourself a few days to reflect upon your decision.’

“‘It would serve no purpose,’ Felix answered. ‘We can never live in your cottage again. My father's life is gravely threatened by the horrifying event I have described to you. My wife and sister will never overcome their terror. I implore you to cease arguing with me. Reclaim your dwelling, and allow me to escape this place.’

“Felix trembled exceedingly as he spoke. He entered the cottage with his companion; they stayed inside a few minutes and then went away. Never again did I behold a member of the De Lacey family.

“For the rest of that day I remained in my shed, sunk in complete, unreasoning despair. My protectors were gone, severing the single bond that joined me to the world. Hatred and the desire for vengeance filled my breast for the first time. I made no effort to master them, but surrendered myself to their current and turned all my thoughts towards destruction and death.”

Yet my father stood beside me to offer comfort and banish painful recollections with cheerful hopes; it seemed sweet to me to mourn, if he might wipe away my tears.

At other times he drew my mind away from its grief by setting it beside his own despair at my mother's death. Even then I trembled at his portrayal of those passions. He possessed a poet's imagination, and in describing the tempest that had torn through his feelings he stamped his language with such vivid life that I believed him as I shuddered. I marvelled that he had ever resumed the duties of ordinary existence after those wild thoughts appeared to have allied him with things beyond this world. The conceptions he communicated as he spoke were so tremendous that a human heart seemed too narrow to contain them. Such feelings belonged more properly to a spirit dwelling amid volcanoes and earthquakes than to one enclosed in mortal flesh and bearing a human form. But they were only recollections; since those days he had altered. Now he was wholly tenderness and love; and when, listening, I lifted wondering eyes towards him, the smile about his mouth assured me that only the mildest passions inhabited his heart.

Two months following my aunt's death we went to London, where my father encouraged me to undertake studies more profound than those I had previously pursued. My progress delighted him. He attended me throughout my studies, helping with or sharing every lesson. We mingled much in society, and he never allowed a day to pass without attempting to adorn it with a fresh pleasure. His tender devotion to me, and the reverent love with which I answered it, lent enchantment to every instant. Time moved slowly, because each minute was put to use; in a single week we experienced more life than many people know in several months, and the freshness and variety of our enjoyments heightened them all.

We were continually going on excursions together. Whether we went to admire lovely scenery, to look upon beautiful paintings, or sometimes merely to find whatever amusement chance might offer, I was happy whenever my father was near. I always regretted the arrival of a third companion; yet if I turned a troubled look upon him, his eyes, resting on me and shining with tenderness, at once brought gladness back to my heart. Oh, hours of such exquisite delight! Though few, you stretch before me like an entire lifetime when I look back through the cloud of sorrow that rose directly afterwards, as though it meant to hide you from my sight.

In my own time and country, this money came from taxes on imports. Citizens liked to imagine that foreign importers paid them. In reality, the American people paid, and the cost was divided so evenly that a man worth a hundred million dollars and a labourer's nursing baby each paid exactly six dollars a year. I suppose nothing could be more equal. Scotland and Ireland paid tribute to Arthur, and the combined population of the British Islands was a little under a million. A skilled worker earned an average of three cents a day, paying his own living expenses. On that basis, the national government spent ninety thousand dollars a year, or roughly two hundred and fifty a day. So by handing out nickels instead of gold on a day for treating the king's evil, I harmed nobody, disappointed nobody, pleased everyone involved, and saved four-fifths of that day's national spending as well. In the America of my time, that saving would have amounted to eight hundred thousand dollars. For this substitution I had consulted wisdom from a distant source: my boyhood. A true statesman values wisdom, however humble its beginnings. As a boy I had always kept my pennies and given buttons to the foreign missionary fund. The ignorant savage would find the buttons as useful as coins, while I found coins more useful than buttons. Everyone was happy, and nobody suffered.

Marinel dealt with the patients as they arrived. He examined each applicant, sent away anyone who did not qualify, and passed the others to the king. A priest read, “They shall lay their hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” While the reading continued, the king stroked the sores. Finally the patient completed the ceremony and received his nickel, which the king himself hung around his neck, before being sent away. Would you imagine that this could cure anyone? It certainly did. Any empty ritual will cure a patient who believes in it strongly enough. Near Astolat stood a chapel where the Virgin had once appeared to a girl who herded geese there—or so the girl herself said. They built the chapel on that spot and hung a painting inside showing what had happened. You would have thought the painting too dreadful for a sick person to go near. Yet every year thousands of sick people and people who could barely walk came to pray in front of it, and left perfectly healthy. Even healthy people could look at it and survive.
